summary: Tiagabine (Gabitril) is an antiseizure medication that boosts the brain’s calming neurotransmitter GABA. In psychiatry, it’s sometimes brought up for anxiety or sleep—but that off-label use has a real seizure risk and isn’t recommended.
description: Tiagabine is FDA-approved only as add-on treatment for focal (partial) seizures in adults and kids age 12+. It increases available GABA, which can feel calming or sedating for some people. Here’s the catch: when tiagabine is used for off-label psychiatric reasons (like anxiety or insomnia), new-onset seizures and even status epilepticus have been reported—even at low doses and even in people without epilepsy. Because of that, tiagabine is generally not a go-to psychiatric med.
patient_summary: Tiagabine is a seizure medication that can feel calming because it increases GABA. But using it for anxiety or sleep (off-label) has been linked to seizures—even in people without a seizure disorder—so it’s usually not recommended for psychiatric use.

secondary.context: Tiagabine has been explored off-label for anxiety because it increases GABA, but off-label use has been linked to new-onset seizures and status epilepticus—even at low doses and even in people without epilepsy. Because of this, psychiatric use is generally not recommended.
It may feel sedating for some people, but using tiagabine for sleep off-label has been associated with seizures. Safer, evidence-based insomnia options are preferred.
Even if the goal is calming or sedation, off-label tiagabine has a seizure risk and is not considered a standard option for psychiatric agitation.

therapeutic_response.display: Fast absorption; peak around 45 minutes fasting (may be delayed with food).

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like lightheadedness, unsteadiness, or a “woozy” brain-body mismatch. It increases fall and accident risk—especially early on or after dose increases.
Sleepiness is common and can hit hard. If you feel overly sedated, your prescriber may slow titration or adjust the dose.
Some people report generalized weakness that can be significant. If it’s intense, dose reduction or stopping can resolve it.
Yes—ironically, an antiseizure med can still make you feel keyed up or edgy. If that happens, it matters clinically because it can look like anxiety worsening.
Brain fog, attention drift, and slower thinking are common complaints. This can impact work/school performance.
Shakiness can range from mild to annoying. If tremor worsens after a dose change, tell your prescriber.
Taking with food can help. Persistent nausea should be reported.

serious_risks.risk: New-onset seizures and status epilepticus (especially when used off-label for non-seizure indications): can occur even at low doses and after dose changes; urgent medical evaluation is needed.
Severe dermatologic reactions (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome): rash with blistering, mucosal sores, fever—medical emergency.
Suicidal ideation/behavior: monitor for mood changes, agitation, hopelessness, or self-harm thoughts.
Severe CNS depression: profound sedation, confusion, ataxia, falls, accidents—risk increases with other sedating meds.
Withdrawal-related seizure worsening if stopped abruptly.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to tiagabine or any component of the formulation

precautions: CNS depression: Can cause dizziness, drowsiness, slowed reaction time, and impaired judgment—use caution with driving and machinery.
Severe skin reactions: Rare but serious reactions (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome) have been reported and can be fatal.
Suicidal thoughts/behavior: Like other antiseizure medications, there is an increased risk of suicidal ideation/behavior; monitor for mood or behavior changes.
Generalized weakness: Sometimes reported as moderately severe to incapacitating; typically improves with dose reduction or stopping.
Ophthalmic uncertainty: Animal data suggest binding in melanin-containing eye tissues; long-term clinical significance is unknown.

interactions.interactant: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone)
interactions.mechanism: Lower tiagabine levels and shorter half-life, which can reduce effect and change dosing needs.
interactions.action: Use the enzyme-inducer dosing approach. If the inducer is added, stopped, or dose-changed, tiagabine usually needs adjustment and sometimes retitration.

interactions.mechanism: May increase tiagabine exposure and side effects (sedation, dizziness, cognitive slowing).
interactions.action: Use caution, monitor closely for CNS side effects, and consider dose reduction if clinically needed.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (alcohol, sedating antihistamines, benzodiazepines, sleep meds, opioids)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, dizziness, impaired coordination, and accident risk.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking sedatives when possible. If combined, go low, go slow, and monitor for impairment.

interactions.interactant: Psych meds in off-label scenarios (antidepressants, antipsychotics, stimulants, opioids)
interactions.mechanism: Off-label tiagabine use alongside these has been reported in cases of new-onset seizures/status epilepticus.
interactions.action: Psychiatric off-label use is not recommended; if seizures occur, discontinue and evaluate for underlying seizure disorder.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidality and mood changes: Monitor for new or worsening depression, irritability, behavioral changes, or suicidal thoughts (risk can appear early).
CNS side effects: Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, memory issues—especially during titration and after medication changes.
Functional safety: Driving risk, work/school performance, falls, accidental injury risk.
Liver function tests: Periodically, especially if there is hepatic impairment or symptoms suggest liver issues.
Seizure activity: If being used for seizures, track seizure frequency; if seizures occur during off-label use, discontinue and evaluate for underlying seizure disorder.
Drug interaction shifts: If enzyme-inducing status changes (starting/stopping an inducer), reassess dose, side effects, and whether retitration is needed.
Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional/clinically targeted): No established therapeutic range, but plasma levels may be useful before and after regimen changes when interactions are likely.

special_populations.pregnancy: Pregnancy data are limited and insufficient to define the risk of specific congenital malformations or neurodevelopmental outcomes. If antiseizure medication is used in pregnancy, monitor fetal growth and screen for major congenital malformations. Track antiseizure medication concentrations and adjust dosing based on seizure control and changing drug levels during pregnancy, then plan a return to pre-pregnancy dosing postpartum. Encourage folic acid supplementation and consider enrollment in the North American Antiepileptic Drug Pregnancy Registry.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if tiagabine is present in breast milk. Limited data exist. The manufacturer recommends use in breastfeeding only when benefits outweigh risks. Monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding/sucking, weight gain, liver function concerns, platelet issues, and developmental milestones; check infant serum concentrations if toxicity is suspected.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing. Start cautiously in older adults due to higher risk of sedation, dizziness, and falls.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No specific manufacturer adjustment is provided, but clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment (unbound clearance decreased ~60% in moderate impairment). Dose reduction may be necessary; titrate slowly and monitor for CNS adverse effects.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid; well absorbed (>95%). Food slows the rate of absorption.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: 7-9 hours; with enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds: 2-5 hours.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food reduces absorption rate (slower rise) but not overall extent; administer with food to reduce rapid plasma increases and CNS effects.

dosing.titration: Tiagabine dosing is built around seizure treatment, not psychiatric symptoms. Because off-label psychiatric use has been linked to seizures, tiagabine is generally not recommended as an anxiety or insomnia medication. If it is used for any reason, dosing must be slow—no loading dose, no rapid titration, and no big dose jumps.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Tiagabine should not be stopped abruptly because it can increase seizure frequency. If it needs to be discontinued, taper gradually unless a safety emergency requires faster action.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Tiagabine (Gabitril) is not a psychiatric medication. It’s FDA-approved only as add-on therapy for focal (partial) seizures in adults and in children age 12 and up. In psychiatry, it sometimes comes up because it increases GABA (the brain’s calming signal), but off-label psychiatric use has been linked to new-onset seizures and status epilepticus—even in people without epilepsy—so it’s generally not recommended.
off_label: Anxiety (off-label; not recommended due to seizure risk)
Insomnia (off-label; not recommended due to seizure risk)
Agitation/sedation (off-label; not recommended due to seizure risk)

sections.intro: People don’t usually take tiagabine for psychiatric symptoms, but when it’s used, these are the kinds of experiences that get reported:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Tiagabine absorbs quickly, but food changes how fast it hits. For psychiatric effects (like sedation), people may notice it relatively soon after a dose—though that’s not an approved use and comes with important risks.
key_points: With food: Absorption rises more slowly (less abrupt peak)
Fasting: Peak levels can occur around 45 minutes
Half-life: ~7-9 hours in adults (shorter—2 to 5 hours—if taking enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds)
Practical tip: It’s typically taken with food to avoid a rapid jump in levels and CNS side effects

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Tiagabine is not an FDA-approved psychiatric treatment, and psychiatric symptom control is not its evidence-based role. Even if someone feels calmer or sleepier on it, off-label psychiatric use is not considered reliably safe because seizures (including status epilepticus) have been reported—even in people without epilepsy.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do not use tiagabine for off-label psychiatric reasons (like anxiety or insomnia). New-onset seizures and status epilepticus have been reported—even at low doses and even without epilepsy.

patient_counseling: Take with food unless your prescriber tells you otherwise—food slows the absorption spike and can reduce side effects.
Don’t drive or do risky tasks until you know how you react—dizziness and drowsiness are common.
If this is being suggested for anxiety or sleep: pause and ask why. Off-label use has been linked to seizures, even in people without epilepsy.
Report rash, blistering, mouth sores, or fever immediately (possible severe skin reaction).
Tell your prescriber right away about new or worsening depression, irritability, or suicidal thoughts.
Don’t stop suddenly without a plan—abrupt withdrawal can increase seizure risk.

sections.intro: Tiagabine is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4. Enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds can dramatically lower tiagabine levels (requiring higher doses), and stopping those inducers can raise tiagabine exposure (requiring dose reduction and careful retitration).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Tiagabine should not be stopped abruptly because it can increase seizure frequency. If it needs to be discontinued, taper gradually unless a safety emergency requires faster action.
key_points: Avoid abrupt discontinuation at any dose—risk of increased seizure frequency.
Adult guidance: Gradual withdrawal over 1 to 6 months is a typical approach unless safety concerns require a more rapid withdrawal.
If multiple doses are missed, your clinician may decide retitration is needed before resuming a full dose.
If enzyme-inducing meds are added or removed during taper, the taper plan may need to be adjusted because tiagabine exposure can shift.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Tiagabine dosing is built around seizure treatment, not psychiatric symptoms. Because off-label psychiatric use has been linked to seizures, tiagabine is generally not recommended as an anxiety or insomnia medication. If it is used for any reason, dosing must be slow—no loading dose, no rapid titration, and no big dose jumps.

adult.not_applicable_psychiatric_dosing: Tiagabine has no established or recommended adult psychiatric dosing. Off-label psychiatric use is not recommended due to reported new-onset seizures and status epilepticus, including in people without epilepsy.

sections.simple_explanation: Tiagabine levels are heavily affected by whether someone is taking enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds. With enzyme inducers, the body clears tiagabine faster, so higher doses may be needed. Without enzyme inducers, levels can be much higher at the same dose—so dosing should be lower and titration slower.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: For psychiatric use, tiagabine isn’t a standard option. If a patient is taking tiagabine for seizure control, pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions should balance seizure risk, medication uncertainty, and shared decision-making with neurology/OB teams.
sections.pregnancy: Pregnancy data are limited and insufficient to define the risk of specific congenital malformations or neurodevelopmental outcomes. If antiseizure medication is used in pregnancy, monitor fetal growth and screen for major congenital malformations. Track antiseizure medication concentrations and adjust dosing based on seizure control and changing drug levels during pregnancy, then plan a return to pre-pregnancy dosing postpartum. Encourage folic acid supplementation and consider enrollment in the North American Antiepileptic Drug Pregnancy Registry.
sections.lactation: It is not known if tiagabine is present in breast milk. Limited data exist. The manufacturer recommends use in breastfeeding only when benefits outweigh risks. Monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding/sucking, weight gain, liver function concerns, platelet issues, and developmental milestones; check infant serum concentrations if toxicity is suspected.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Start cautiously in older adults due to higher risk of sedation, dizziness, and falls.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer adjustment is provided, but clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment (unbound clearance decreased ~60% in moderate impairment). Dose reduction may be necessary; titrate slowly and monitor for CNS adverse effects.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and mood changes: Monitor for new or worsening depression, irritability, behavioral changes, or suicidal thoughts (risk can appear early).
CNS side effects: Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, memory issues—especially during titration and after medication changes.
Functional safety: Driving risk, work/school performance, falls, accidental injury risk.
Liver function tests: Periodically, especially if there is hepatic impairment or symptoms suggest liver issues.
Seizure activity: If being used for seizures, track seizure frequency; if seizures occur during off-label use, discontinue and evaluate for underlying seizure disorder.
Drug interaction shifts: If enzyme-inducing status changes (starting/stopping an inducer), reassess dose, side effects, and whether retitration is needed.
Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional/clinically targeted): No established therapeutic range, but plasma levels may be useful before and after regimen changes when interactions are likely.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Tiagabine is available as oral tablets. Brand-name Gabitril is discontinued in the US, but generics are available.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Tiagabine increases the amount of GABA available in the brain by blocking GABA reuptake (inhibits the GABA uptake carrier). More GABA hanging around means more inhibitory, “calming” signaling—helpful for seizure control, but not reliably safe or appropriate as a psychiatric calming agent because of the seizure risk reported with off-label use.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, tiagabine is a classic “sounds calming on paper” medication that doesn’t belong in routine anxiety or insomnia treatment. Yes, it increases GABA. But off-label use has been associated with new-onset seizures and status epilepticus, including in people without epilepsy—often alongside common psych meds. So in real-world psychiatric algorithms, tiagabine is generally a no. If someone is already on tiagabine for seizures and develops anxiety or insomnia, treat the psychiatric symptoms with evidence-based options that don’t add seizure risk, and coordinate with neurology before any antiseizure med changes.

faqs.a: It’s been tried off-label because it increases GABA (a calming brain signal), but it’s not recommended. Off-label use has been linked to new-onset seizures and status epilepticus—even in people without epilepsy and even at low doses—so it’s not a standard anxiety treatment.

faqs.q: Can tiagabine help with sleep or insomnia?
faqs.a: Some people feel sleepy on it, but using tiagabine for insomnia is not recommended because off-label use has been associated with seizures. If sleep is the problem, safer, evidence-based insomnia treatments are preferred.

faqs.q: Why would a “calming” medication cause seizures?
faqs.a: Tiagabine changes inhibitory signaling by increasing available GABA. When used outside its approved seizure-treatment context—especially alongside other medications that affect the brain—seizures have been reported in some patients. That’s why psychiatric off-label use is considered risky.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Dizziness and drowsiness are the big ones. Weakness, tremor, nausea, and trouble concentrating are also common. These effects can affect driving, coordination, and work/school performance.

faqs.q: Does tiagabine interact with other medications?
faqs.a: Yes. Enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications can lower tiagabine levels and shorten its half-life (often requiring higher doses). If those inducers are stopped, tiagabine exposure can rise, increasing side effects—so dose changes may require careful adjustment or retitration.

faqs.q: Should tiagabine be taken with food?
faqs.a: Yes—typically with food. Food slows how fast tiagabine is absorbed, which can reduce a rapid spike in levels and may lower the chance of CNS side effects.
No. Abrupt discontinuation can increase seizure frequency. If it needs to be stopped, it should be tapered gradually unless a safety concern requires faster withdrawal.

faqs.q: Is there a therapeutic blood level for tiagabine?
faqs.a: There isn’t an established therapeutic range. That said, because tiagabine is sensitive to drug interactions (especially enzyme inducers/inhibitors), clinicians may check levels before and after regimen changes in some cases.

faqs.q: Is tiagabine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Pregnancy outcome data are limited, so risks aren’t well defined. If it’s being used for seizure control, pregnancy decisions should prioritize seizure stability and involve shared decision-making with neurology and OB teams. For breastfeeding, it’s unknown if tiagabine is present in breast milk; infant monitoring is recommended if used.
